issues.title: Extremal-subspace threshold in Algorithm 2

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In all the experiments we have conducted for various $n$ and $k$, this value was equal to $\arccos(1 / \sqrt{n})$.

issues.failure_explanation: The value d is the least largest-principal-angle deviation, whose conjectured extremal value is arccos(1/sqrt(n)). For n=2 and k=1, the line spanned by (1,1) has d=pi/4. For any 0<epsilon<pi/4-1/sqrt(2), the displayed upper predicate is true, so the algorithm announces that the hypothesis is false and returns -1 even though this input is exactly at the conjectured angle bound. The lower predicate is centered on the same wrong scale and can likewise classify nonextremal values as extremal.
issues.overall_effect: Taken literally, Algorithm 2 cannot reliably distinguish extremal candidates from counterexamples and can fail to return the promised set even on an exact extremal input. The formal theorem does not depend on this pseudocode.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define theta_n=arccos(1/sqrt(n)) and center both tests in Algorithm 2 at theta_n: use d>theta_n+epsilon for declaring a counterexample and d>theta_n-epsilon for accepting a candidate as extremal, with epsilon measured on the same angular scale as Distance. No other part of the algorithm or any formal result needs alteration.
issues.why_classification: The old source unambiguously defines d as a largest-principal-angle target and explicitly identifies arccos(1/sqrt(n)) as the conjectured extremal value, so the correction is short, local, routine, and source-supported. It is not merely harmless typography because the erroneous quantity controls executable branches and can cause a false return. The correction preserves the intended algorithmic contract and entails no mathematical loss or dependent-proof repair, making the issue minor.
